questions.note: Four free checks: chest, urine dipstick, glucose, scrotum in boys.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old hits the handlebars of his bike, has left upper quadrant pain, and is discharged after observation with stable vital signs. Two days later he collapses with tachycardia and hypotension. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Rupture of a traumatic pancreatic pseudocyst
Obstruction from an intramural duodenal haematoma
Delayed perforation of the transverse colon
Delayed rupture of a subcapsular splenic haematoma
questions.explain: Two-stage splenic rupture occurs when a subcapsular haematoma expands and then ruptures hours to days after injury, causing haemorrhagic shock. A duodenal haematoma causes bilious vomiting, a pseudocyst forms over weeks, and perforation causes peritonitis rather than sudden shock.
questions.note: Two-stage splenic rupture: subcapsular haematoma, shock hours to days later.

questions.stem: A 10-day-old baby born at 29 weeks develops feed intolerance, abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and bloody stools. Abdominal X-ray shows intramural gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: A preterm neonate with distension, bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis has necrotising enterocolitis, one of the two key neonatal acute abdomens with volvulus. Hirschsprung enterocolitis occurs mainly in term babies with delayed meconium, and meconium ileus presents at birth.
questions.note: Sort by age: neonate NEC and volvulus; toddler intussusception; school age appendicitis.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has 24 hours of right lower quadrant pain with guarding and rebound tenderness. HR is 118/min, BP 102/64 mmHg, and capillary refill 2 seconds. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with oral antibiotics and safety-netting advice
Urgent surgical referral with IV fluids and analgesia
Give laxatives and reassess in 24 hours
Arrange outpatient ultrasound within a week
questions.explain: Peritonism (guarding, rebound) mandates surgical referral, with resuscitation, analgesia and IV antibiotics as needed. Analgesia does not mask signs and should never be withheld; outpatient imaging or laxatives risk perforation.
questions.note: Peritonism → surgical referral; resuscitate if unstable.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old has severe left testicular pain for 4 hours with vomiting. The testis lies high and horizontally, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explain: Clinical testicular torsion goes straight to theatre, because salvage falls sharply after about 6 hours; ultrasound should not delay surgery when the diagnosis is clinically clear. Manual detorsion is only a temporising measure and still requires bilateral fixation.
questions.note: Salvage of a torted testis falls sharply after about 6 hours.

cards.front: List the causes of acute abdomen in children by age.
cards.back: Neonate: NEC, malrotation/volvulus • toddler: intussusception • school age: appendicitis • adolescent: testicular/ovarian torsion, ectopic and other gynaecological causes • any age: trauma (splenic rupture), DKA, pneumonia.

cards.front: What are the 'four free checks' in a child with abdominal pain, and why?
cards.back: Chest (lower lobe pneumonia) • urine dipstick (UTI, glucose) • blood glucose (DKA) • scrotum in boys (torsion).

cards.front: Why does appendicitis pain start periumbilically, and what are the classic features?
cards.back: Appendix is a midgut organ; visceral afferents enter the cord at T10 → periumbilical pain, then parietal peritoneum irritation → RLQ • anorexia, low fever, guarding.

I-30.summary: With a childhood abdominal mass, first exclude benign causes (bladder, stool, hydronephrosis), then separate the well 3-year-old with a smooth flank mass that respects the midline (Wilms) from the unwell toddler whose mass crosses it (neuroblastoma). Image with ultrasound and do not keep palpating.

questions.stem: What is the commonest origin of an abdominal mass in a newborn?
options: Hepatic, such as hepatoblastoma or infantile hepatic haemangioma
Renal, such as hydronephrosis or multicystic dysplastic kidney
Adrenal, such as neuroblastoma or haemorrhage
Intestinal, such as a duplication cyst
questions.explain: Most neonatal abdominal masses are renal, most often hydronephrosis (for example pelviureteric junction obstruction) or multicystic dysplastic kidney. Neuroblastoma and hepatic tumours are much rarer.
questions.note: Neonate: most masses are renal (hydronephrosis, multicystic dysplastic kidney).

questions.stem: A well 3-year-old girl has a smooth left flank mass found by her mother at bath time. It does not cross the midline, there is microscopic haematuria, and BP is raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: A smooth unilateral flank mass in a well child aged 3-4 years with haematuria and hypertension is Wilms tumour. Neuroblastoma usually affects children under 2 who are unwell, with an irregular mass crossing the midline, and MCDK presents in the neonate.
questions.note: Wilms: peaks 3-4 years, well child, smooth mass, does not cross the midline, haematuria.

questions.stem: A miserable 18-month-old has weight loss, bilateral periorbital bruising, and a hard, irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline. Which urine test supports the diagnosis?
questions.explain: An unwell toddler with a midline-crossing mass and 'raccoon eyes' (orbital metastases) has neuroblastoma; its catecholamine metabolites VMA and HVA are raised in the urine. 5-HIAA is raised in carcinoid, and beta-hCG in germ cell tumours.
questions.note: Neuroblastoma: raised urinary VMA and HVA; small blue round cells, Homer-Wright rosettes.

questions.stem: What is the first-line imaging investigation for a palpable abdominal mass in a child?
questions.explain: Ultrasound is quick, radiation-free and identifies the organ of origin, whether the mass is cystic or solid, and vascular involvement (for example tumour thrombus in the IVC). CT or MRI follows for staging.
questions.note: Abdominal ultrasound first.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has absent irises bilaterally, hypospadias with undescended testes, and developmental delay. Which tumour requires regular ultrasound surveillance?
questions.explain: Aniridia with genitourinary anomalies and intellectual disability is WAGR syndrome (11p13 deletion including WT1), which carries a high risk of Wilms tumour, so renal ultrasound surveillance is performed. Aniridia is not associated with retinoblastoma.
questions.note: Wilms: WAGR (aniridia), Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, hemihypertrophy; neuroblastoma: neural crest, N-myc.

questions.stem: On a teaching ward round, a 3-year-old with a newly found smooth renal mass is admitted, and several students ask to examine her abdomen. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Allow each student a gentle examination
Perform deep palpation to assess mobility
Restrict abdominal palpation to a single senior examination
Allow the students to examine her only after sedating the child
questions.explain: Repeated palpation of a suspected Wilms tumour risks capsular rupture and tumour spillage, which upstages the disease and worsens prognosis. Examination should be limited, and imaging used to define the mass.
questions.note: A suspected Wilms tumour must not be repeatedly palpated.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has a confirmed Wilms tumour. Which site is the commonest location of distant metastases, and so must be imaged at staging?
questions.explain: Wilms tumour arises from metanephric blastema and spreads mainly haematogenously to the lungs, so chest CT is part of staging. Bone marrow, skeletal and orbital metastases are characteristic of neuroblastoma.
questions.note: Wilms arises from metanephric mesenchyme (blastema); it spreads mostly to the lungs.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old in a European centre has an imaging-confirmed unilateral Wilms tumour without metastases. Under the SIOP protocol, what is the standard initial treatment?
questions.explain: SIOP (Europe) gives preoperative chemotherapy (vincristine ± actinomycin D) to shrink the tumour and reduce rupture risk before nephrectomy. The North American COG approach usually operates first, then stages and treats.
questions.note: Europe (SIOP): chemotherapy before surgery; US (COG): usually operate first.

cards.front: How do you distinguish Wilms tumour from neuroblastoma?
cards.back: Wilms: 3-4 y, well, smooth flank mass, does not cross midline, haematuria, HTN, lung mets • Neuroblastoma: < 2 y, unwell, irregular mass crosses midline, raccoon eyes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, raised VMA/HVA, bone mets.

cards.front: List the genetic associations of Wilms tumour and neuroblastoma.
cards.back: Wilms: WAGR (aniridia, WT1), Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia, organomegaly), hemihypertrophy, Denys-Drash • Neuroblastoma: neural crest origin, N-myc amplification = poor prognosis; Homer-Wright rosettes.

cards.front: How do you approach an abdominal mass in a child?
cards.back: Exclude benign causes (bladder, faeces, hydronephrosis/MCDK in neonates) • ultrasound first • do not palpate repeatedly • urinary VMA/HVA • CT/MRI staging • Wilms: SIOP chemo first vs COG surgery first.
